articles.title: UN warns monster El Niño could push 49 million more people into hunger
articles.raw_rss: Global acute food insecurity projected to rise to 274 million people across 45 countries, WFP says
articles.raw_meta: Global acute food insecurity projected to rise to 274 million people across 45 countries, WFP says
articles.jina_text:
A powerful El Niño weather pattern could push nearly 49 million more people into acute hunger by the end of next year, the U.N. World Food Programme warned Wednesday, raising fears of worsening food shortages across some of the world's most vulnerable regions.
The agency said there is an 81% chance of a very strong El Niño developing, with Pacific Ocean temperatures on track to reach their highest levels since at least 1982. If forecasts hold, it could become the strongest El Niño since 1950, triggering widespread droughts, floods and erratic rainfall that threaten food production.
Based on an assessment of 45 countries most vulnerable to El Niño, the WFP estimates the number of people facing acute food insecurity could climb by almost 49 million, bringing the total to about 274 million. Central America and Southern Africa are expected to be among the hardest-hit regions, with food insecurity projected to increase by 83% and nearly 75%, respectively. Southern Africa, South America and the Caribbean could each see more than 12 million additional people fall into acute hunger.





open image in gallery
Tourists cool off at a public water fountain in Paris, June 26 (Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.)
"These are events that in the past have triggered large-scale hunger," Jean-Martin Bauer, director of the WFP's Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Service, told reporters.





Bauer said global food supplies are entering the El Niño period in relatively good shape after strong harvests in recent years, but warned that conflict in the Middle East and weather-related crop losses could still drive up food prices and make it harder for vulnerable families to afford basic staples.

The WFP also warned that funding cuts from the United States and Europe are making it harder to track emerging hunger crises. Bauer described a growing shortage of food security data, saying the agency conducted about 1.1 million household surveys in 2024 but only around 800,000 this year because of reduced funding.





open image in gallery
A woman fetches drinking water from an unprotected well, as Zimbabwe is experiencing an El Nino-induced drought (Reuters)
"At a time when you have a risk like an El Niño, it is important to have high-frequency data collection," Bauer said, warning that weaker monitoring could delay the response to worsening food emergencies.


Current forecasts point to below-average rainfall across parts of East Africa, the Sahel, Central America and the Caribbean, while flooding risks are expected to rise in Somalia and neighboring countries. Parts of South and Southeast Asia could also face drought, disrupted monsoons and localized flooding that threaten crop production.



The WFP said it has already expanded anticipatory aid programs in 18 countries, reaching more than 1.3 million people this year with cash assistance and other support designed to lessen the impact of extreme weather before disaster strikes.

articles.title: New car sales surge in UK amid electric vehicle revolution
articles.jina_text:
New car registrations in the UK increased by 11.7 per cent in July, marking the eighth consecutive month of growth, with a total of 156,571 vehicles registered according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). 
Demand for electric vehicles (EVs) was a significant driver of this growth, rising by 44.5 per cent to 43,106 cars, now accounting for 14.9 per cent of the car market, while plug-in hybrids also saw a 33.6 per cent increase. 
Conversely, registrations for diesel and petrol cars experienced declines, dropping by 5.2 per cent and 17.7 per cent respectively during the same period. 
Growth was observed across all car buying sectors, with private buyer uptake increasing by 12.6 per cent and fleet deliveries rising by 9.5 per cent, representing six in ten registrations. 
The SMMT forecasts that electric vehicles will achieve a 27.4 per cent market share by the end of the year, though chief executive Mike Hawes expressed concerns that manufacturers are facing financial strain from EV discounts, which could jeopardise future investment and viability despite the industry's commitment to decarbonisation.

articles.title: How the future of British farming is transforming due to climate change
articles.raw_rss: Heatwaves could allow farmers to consider new crops that previously ‘we could never imagine’ growing in the UK
articles.raw_meta: Heatwaves could allow farmers to consider new crops that previously ‘we could never imagine’ growing in the UK
articles.jina_text:
With drought conditions declared across half of England, British farmers are continuing to face the extreme effects of climate change. 
Amid increasing reports of reduced crop yields and predicted food shortages, growers across the country are rushing to adapt to what the Met Office has termed the “new normal”.
With several heatwaves and temperature records broken over the last few weeks, these conditions have contributed to what has been recognised as “one of the worst harvests in living memory”.





With typical British produce such as sweetcorn, green beans, garden peas, and broccoli beginning to struggle, some experts have suggested the warmer temperatures are an opportunity for Britain to diversify its fruit and vegetable production. 
Here, The Independent finds out what crops could one day be grown in the UK, potentially changing the future of farming across the country.






open image in gallery
For farmers across the country, climate change has become ‘a constant reality’ (AFP/Getty)

Fruit 
Charlie Taverner, policy lead at the Food, Farming and Countryside Commission, said: “Climate change has become a constant reality that our farmers are grappling with – they’re at the forefront of this all.


“But while we’re seeing an awful lot of apprehension, we have to see the opportunity. Some crops that we could never even imagine growing here are now becoming viable.” 
He suggested a wider variety of fruit trees, olives and grapes are starting to become more viable in the UK without the use of polytunnels.



“Things which traditionally grow in warmer, Mediterranean climates are now showing more potential to be grown here,” Mr Taverner said.

Vegetables
For vegetable growers, this summer has been particularly hard, as leafy greens, carrots and pumpkins are among those which have seen large declines in yield. 





But Liz Mooney from the Royal Horticultural Society said: “The climate is definitely having a major impact on what agriculture in the UK could look like in the future. 
“Sweet potatoes, sweet peppers, artichokes and chillies are all vegetables that are now able to grow here, without the need for greenhouses or extra equipment.”
She added even tomatoes, which usually have to be grown in temperature-controlled conditions, are now showing success when grown outside.





open image in gallery
The heat has allowed a larger variety of vegetables to be grown in the UK without extra equipment (AFP/Getty)
But she emphasised the potential of these crops is not based on warm weather alone. 
“If we want to be able to grow anything, we need to ensure we’re doing our best to protect our soil, practice sustainability, and diversify what we’re planting – if we do that, then something will always grow well,” Ms Mooney said.

Legumes
Legumes, which the UK predominantly imports from South America and Asia, are similarly showing viability for growth domestically.

Chris Bowen vows to override Queensland and NT to force renewables-powered AI datacentres


Energy minister says Australian households and energy reliability will be protected by new federal legislation 




Energy minister Chris Bowen says the federal government will override state governments that oppose new national rules on datacentres, with commonwealth legislation forcing new AI datacentres to be powered by renewable energy and banning those fuelled by gas.
Bowen said he expected his counterparts in Queensland and the Northern Territory – who had protested the new federal rules at a meeting last week – to be unhappy with the move, but said the Albanese government was committed to powering the AI revolution with renewable energy.

“We will legislate as a commonwealth. The constitution is clear about the power of commonwealth legislation. I respectfully disagree with Queensland and the Northern Territory,” Bowen told the National Press Club on Wednesday.



The Australian Energy Market Commission warned that without rule changes such as those proposed by Bowen, the costs of bringing large datacentres online “will be paid for in part by customers” rather than big tech companies.
Prime minister Anthony Albanese ast month pledged to legislate binding standards for AI datacentres, including on locations and energy use, with new national rules requiring them to rely on new renewable energy, minimise water use and maximise energy efficiency, pay for their grid connection costs and “put at least as much energy into our grid as they take out of it”.
Queensland and the NT last week opposed the changes in a meeting of state and federal energy ministers, despite all other states backing the plan. Queensland’s David Janetzki called the federal proposal “underdeveloped ideas that hand increased power to Canberra”.
The NT has proposed a major datacentre powered by gas from the controversial Beetaloo basin development.
But Bowen on Wednesday confirmed federal legislation would mandate the rules set out by Albanese. He said while gas had a “role to play” in firming up datacentre power use, “if a datacentre is proposed to only use gas, it will not meet the national minimum standards and it will not be allowed to register and will not be able to proceed”.


“While I always prefer to work with my state and territory colleagues, the commonwealth will not be standing by and letting a race to the bottom of states falling over themselves to attract datacentres, at the cost to household bills, reliability or emissions,” he said.

El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next year 


UN forecasters warn of worsening conditions in 45 countries currently experiencing severe food insecurity




About 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by the rapidly developing El Niño weather system, according to forecasting.
This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts of Africa and pressure on food prices from the war in Iran.

Even if the forecast El Niño is less strong than some models predict, it will tip many countries over the edge, adding more than a fifth to the 225 million people in 45 countries currently in acute food insecurity, the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Wednesday.
Central and South America, the Caribbean and southern Africa are likely to be worst affected, according to the analysis. In south and south-east Asia there is likely to be less rainfall than usual, which would cause serious problems for agriculture and farmers.







India’s monsoon rains in danger as UN chief warns planet is ‘on fire’

This year’s El Niño – a weather system that develops every few years in the Pacific Ocean and brings changes to rainfall patterns around the world – is shaping up to be the strongest in at least 70 years. Some are calling it a “super El Niño”, though this term is not officially recognised.

What is certain is that its impacts and strength are being strongly affected by the climate crisis. Earlier this year, experts said a strong El Niño could work in tandem with global heating to deliver the hottest year on record either this year or, more likely, in 2027.


Private sector forecasters have already warned of the impact of the gathering El Niño on global food prices, but the report published by the WFP is the first to look closely at global hunger. The WFP said it was hoping to reduce the effects of the extreme weather through early warning systems and “anticipatory” relief efforts, for which at least $80m (£60m) is budgeted.
The consequences will still be far-reaching, as farmers may take more than one season to exhaust their food supplies. In southern Africa, for instance, the main growing season stretches from October this year to March 2027, but it will be about nine months later, during the lean season following the harvest, that the worst impacts will bite.

articles.title: Companies still ignoring nature loss as world misses almost all its 2030 targets, says UN biodiversity chief
articles.raw_rss: Biodiversity loss has appeared among World Economic Forum's top global risks every year since 2020
articles.raw_meta: Biodiversity loss has appeared among World Economic Forum
articles.jina_text:
Companies are failing to act on the loss of nature despite knowing for years that it threatens their supply chains and profits, the head of the UN's biodiversity body has said.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, told Reuters that while some firms were closely engaged, many remained "on the sidelines" as governments prepare for a summit that will review targets the UN's own draft report says are almost all being missed.
"Companies are not investing enough time and energy and resources into analysing their biodiversity impacts and dependencies and risk along the supply chain," she said, speaking before preparatory talks in Nairobi this week.





Biodiversity loss has appeared among the World Economic Forum's top global risks every year since 2020, a list drawn from surveys of business leaders and used widely in corporate planning.
"The paradox is that biodiversity and nature risk has been amongst the top risks for the past five or six years," Ms Schomaker told Reuters. 

"So in a way they are aware that there's a risk, but companies are not yet acting on it."
She said the delay was due to practical and financial obstacles, with firms slow to assess their exposure while governments are slow to require them to disclose it. 


Nature risk remains harder to measure than carbon emissions because it is specific to place, so a company's exposure depends on which river, forest or fishery its operations and suppliers depend on rather than on a single global figure.



A gaviao caramujeiro, snail kite (Rostrhamus sociabilis) is pictured at the Pantanal, a key region along birds' migratory routes in the Americas, in the municipality of Miranda in Mato Grosso do Sul state, Brazil (AFP/Getty)
The Armenia summit, the 17th meeting of the parties to the convention, will carry out the first full review of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the agreement struck in Montreal in 2022 under which almost every country committed to protect 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, restore damaged ecosystems and cut subsidies that harm nature. 



Every country in the world is party to the convention except the United States and the Holy See. 
A draft of the UN's own global report on progress, published last week, found countries falling short on 22 of the framework's 23 targets and warned that the goal of halting and reversing nature loss by 2030 would not be met unless action accelerated rapidly. 
The draft has been through peer review and will be edited before publication ahead of the summit.
One target has already passed. Countries were meant to identify all their subsidies that damage nature by 2025, as the first step towards cutting $500bn of them a year by 2030. 

Analysis by Carbon Brief of 134 national reports found that 21 countries appear to have done so, about 16 per cent of those that have reported, while 62 countries have not submitted a report at all.

This, roughly speaking, is how the dismissal of climate action is now being justified: the argument has shifted from science denial to outright nihilism.

In a column in the Daily Telegraph last week, originally titled “Britain can’t stop climate change. I’m not qualified to diagnose people, but as a general rule, a lack of empathy, alongside callousness and an absence of guilt, is a strong indicator of a psychopath. Yes, he continued, “there will be plenty of losers, but it is pointless seeking to prevent the inevitable … Many in Britain would enjoy the kind of warmer climate predicted by modellers”.

articles.jina_text:
As rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administered Kashmir. His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier.
“I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, a cloudburst sent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside.

Latief, 48, had spent years building the house, where five generations of his Gujjar family lived together. Within minutes, the torrent swallowed it, trapping eight family members inside. He survived only because he had stepped outside. By dawn, everything he had built lay in rubble.
When the Guardian reached Murrah four days later, electricity, roads and mobile networks were cut off. Floodwaters had washed away roads and footbridges, leaving the only way into the village a 90-minute walk through rain and landslide debris. Residents carried sacks of flour, cooking gas cylinders and medicines across the broken crossing.
Murrah is perched high in the Pir Panjal range above the town of Bafliaz, in Poonch district, about 125 miles (200km) south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir’s main city. The village is home to mostly Gujjars, one of the largest pastoralist communities in the Himalayas, whose livelihoods have long depended on livestock, farming and seasonal migration through the mountains.
The hillside remained too unstable for excavators to reach. Soldiers, disaster response teams and local volunteers searched the debris by hand while others combed the swollen Suran River for the missing.


View image in fullscreen
Rescue teams search for missing people in Murrah village after the cloudburst-triggered landslide. Photograph: Ishtayaq Rasool


Latief now lives in the house of his brother, Mohd Bashir, just above the landslide. Inside, women gathered to mourn while men quietly received visitors offering condolences. Verses from the Qur’an echoed through the house.
“I built that house for my family,” Latief said, holding up pictures of his 16-year-old son Sajjad Ahmed, an aspiring cricketer, whose body was still missing. Days before the disaster, the family recorded videos together.


View image in fullscreen
A photograph on a phone of 16-year-old Sajjad Ahmed, whose body remains missing Photograph: Ishtayaq Rasool
As mourners gathered, news spread that another body had been found several miles down the river; the room fell silent as another funeral procession passed through the village.


Among those searching was Mohammad Razak, 45, who had spent four days combing the river with a team of volunteers. “We’ve been searching every bend of the river,” he said. “We’re still hoping we’ll find them.”

Iran conflict windfall over three months reignites calls for companies ‘cashing in on human misery’ to pay for environmental damage













 
 
Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.

The windfall war profits have reignited calls for oil and gas supermajors such as Saudi Aramco and BP to pay for the environmental damage caused by “cashing in on human misery” and fund a rapid transition to renewable energy.
Guardian analysis found that the eight listed oil producers made almost $93bn (£69bn) in the three months to the end of June – the first full financial quarter after the US-Israeli war on Iran triggered a surge in global oil prices to highs above $126 a barrel.

The companies have used the biggest disruption of fossil fuel supplies in the market’s history to almost double their combined profits from just under $50bn in the same period last year, with campaigners warning that millions of households are left paying the price in higher bills and climate chaos.


The data suggests the eight oil companies – Aramco, BP, Shell, Equinor, TotalEnergies, Eni, Chevron and ExxonMobil – made more than $700,000 of profit every minute over the spring quarter.
While their market valuations were swelling by about $600bn to above $3tn, temperatures built towards a run of deadly heatwaves, all made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels.
Carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel firms were directly linked to fatal spells of hot weather for the first time by scientific analysis published last September. It found the emissions from any one of the 14 biggest companies were each enough to cause more than 50 heatwaves that would otherwise have been virtually impossible.


View image in fullscreen
Blackheath in south London, a wide open common usually known for its sweeping green spaces and views, has been left looking scorched and barren by the severe drought that was officially declared across more than half of England in late July 2026. Photograph: Fraser Gray/Shutterstock
The biggest oil profits in the spring quarter were raked in by Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company, Aramco, which reported a 34% increase in its quarterly net income to more than $33bn, even as its infrastructure was damaged by drone and missile strikes from Iranian and Houthi forces.

articles.jina_text:
Far beyond the fires raging across Europe and North America, the smoke, dangerous to breathe, hangs in the air, dimming the view, changing the very color of sunlight into something grimly unsettling.
An estimated 20,000 are said to have died in the extreme heat in Europe earlier this year, and heat is climate change’s quiet killer, compared with the dramatic violence of death by fire or flood. In eastern Washington, 600 homes have just burned down, and in both Europe and North America, firefighters have died in the effort to contain the climate-fueled firestorms.

Once, across much of the the world’s temperate zones, we looked forward to summer as a time of delights, from summer’s bounty of fruits, long days, warmth, school holidays, activities like camping and swimming, travel and adventure. Now many of us dread it.






Wildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonder
Bill McGuire


Read more
Summer was the sweet season celebrated in poetry and song, often pictured as a gentle goddess; now it is too often a threat and a misery. All this makes me think of Bill McKibben’s 2011 book Eaarth, a proposal that we can understand climate change as equivalent to moving to a more perilous, unwelcoming planet than the gentle, stable one we evolved over the 12,000 years since the last ice age.
I know that there are parts of the world where summer was already harsh, intense – 20 years ago, my friend Mark Klett, a photographer living near Phoenix, Arizona, joked: “Phoenix has two seasons: summer and hell,” summer being January and February; hell being the rest of the year.


But even in Phoenix, summer is now more intense; there, people get severe burns from falling down on superheated asphalt. It’s changed everywhere.
I’ve driven to New Mexico almost every summer since 1989. A few years ago, I found that I feared heat for the first time: the temperature in Needles, a California desert town on the Colorado River near the Arizona border, was going to be 116F (46.6C). I didn’t know if my car could survive temperatures like that, and I feared what survival would look like for me if the air-conditioned car broke down on the highway. (I managed it by staying on the edge of the Mojave Desert the night before and darting across the low desert to Flagstaff, which at 7,000ft elevation stays cooler, and pressing on to New Mexico the next day.)
I’m in New Mexico now, as I write, enjoying the beauties of its incomparable skies and summer thunderstorms, but 37 summers since I started coming, summer is not what it used to be. It’s hotter.
The monsoon rains are less reliable and often more violent when they come; one New Mexico town, Ruidoso, has over the past few years been beaten up repeatedly by flood and fire. A gardener accustomed to the sprawling landscapes of Tuscan estates and iconic British gardens like Sissinghurst is now demonstrating how even the smallest urban spaces can become vital havens for biodiversity. 
Thomas Rutter, whose professional career has spanned prestigious locations including Lowther Castle and Iford Manor, cultivates a thriving 5m x 1m balcony garden on the fourth floor of his Tottenham flat.
Rutter's personal project serves as compelling evidence that people with limited outdoor areas can significantly contribute to local ecosystems. 





"Any small space, whether it’s a window ledge or a crack in the wall or a balcony, or something larger like a small terrace, all have value," explains the 35-year-old, whose latest book, The Ethical Gardener, champions this very approach.
He highlights simple yet effective methods. "I have a small number of pots on some saucers which are full of water. I can’t tell you the number of birds that have visited my balcony in the last week for water."

A new Green London council leader has said he wants to make it “more difficult” for people to drive their cars as he laid out his vision for the borough. 




Jame McAsh outlined his plans for Southwark, including increasing affordable housing, tackling the climate emergency and resisting immigration raids. 








He said that some measures his administration will propose will be controversial but insisted he is willing to make “difficult choices” to improve the lives of residents. 




“Londoners are dying from extreme heat, and when it comes to the winter, we'll be expecting extreme weather in other ways, flooding, etc,” Mr McAsh told the Standard. 




“So we need to react to that. But being a Green is also about kind of the space that we're in. 




“So we want to see a lot more trees. We want to make it safer for kids to walk and cycle to school, and that means reducing traffic. 




“It means taking action to, you know, not just make it easy to walk and cycle, but also make it more difficult to drive your car around. 












“And sometimes those are difficult choices. But if that's what we believe, we kind of need to take those kinds of actions.”


James McAsh
JamesMcAsh




Changing the way people travel around the borough could include blocking off “rat runs” and increasing the number of low traffic neighbourhoods (LTNs) and school streets, Mr McAsh said. 








He added: “Tony Benn, a hero of mine, talked about a signpost and weather vanes, and a weather vane moves around in the wind, and a signpost points the right direction. 




“And I firmly believe that yes, we need to engage the community. Yes, we need to talk to people about how we're doing things.

articles.jina_text:
Good morning. Half of England and all of Wales are officially in drought, wildfires have burned through parts of the Cairngorms, Suffolk and the Isle of Wight, and reservoirs are running low. Farmers have warned that there could soon be food shortages, and the Royal Horticultural Society is considering moving its hydrangeas to cope with the heat. Many people are now asking a question rarely associated with British summertime: when will it rain?
The Guardian has been covering how the climate crisis is supercharging wildfires in Europe, the impossible choices firefighters face about which places to save, the number of people who have died in England due to heat, and the air conditioning haves and have-nots. Had you been reading another newspaper, you may have come away with a very different impression of this extreme weather.



Over the last week, a string of articles, mostly in the Telegraph, suggested that Britain should give up on net zero and learn to live with its newly Mediterranean climate; that wildfires had been exacerbated by environmental groups; and, rather grandiosely, that climate “catastrophism” is a “leftist weapon” designed to “destroy capitalism”.
In a week when England entered its fourth heatwave of 2026, this line of argument might have seemed more than a little out of touch. But it reflects how climate deniers are reconfiguring their narratives in the face of an indisputable crisis. I spoke to Bob Ward, policy and communications director at the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change, about how a minority is shaping the political debate and trying to thwart the transition, even while most people want to see more action on climate. First, here are the headlines.
Five big stories
 
 
UK news | Rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded from early release plans to ease critical prison overcrowding in a major intervention by Andy Burnham. 
 
UK politics | Nigel Farage has made his clearest admission that he was in talks to return to lead Reform UK months before the 2024 general election, casting fresh doubt on previous claims that he was not involved in politics when he received a £5m gift. 
 
Spain | A growing chorus of voices has accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”. 
 
Middle East | New talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday. 
 
Environment | A plastic manufacturer in the north of England is facing potential legal action over emissions of benzene, a carcinogenic chemical with no safe level, the Guardian can reveal. 
In depth: From ‘lukewarmers’ to ‘daft’ arguments – how climate deniers are reshaping political discourse

articles.jina_text:
Exclusive: Environment Agency is considering whether to prosecute Huntsman Polyurethanes over emissions of carcinogenic benzene




A plastic manufacturer in the north of England is facing potential legal action over emissions of benzene, a carcinogenic chemical with no safe level, the Guardian can reveal.
The Environment Agency (EA) is considering taking legal action against Huntsman Polyurethanes in Teesside for a potential breach of licence, which is a criminal offence.

Campaigners say it has shone a light on the toxic nature of the global plastics industry and that workers and the local community have been put at risk.
Huntsman Polyurethanes, a petrochemical company that manufactures chemicals to produce plastic, sits within the sprawling Teesside chemical cluster in the seaside town of Redcar, North Yorkshire. The factory is part of Huntsman Corporation, a publicly traded global producer and marketer of chemical products which boasted revenues of $6bn in 2025.
In 2023, Huntsman decommissioned a process that was reducing its benzene air emissions and replaced it with an alternative method controlled by a third party.
However, EA documents show this new process “periodically paused”, with benzene consequently emitted directly to the air. The documents also show the EA was aware of this problem in 2023, but did not investigate until this year.
During this time, the benzene emissions from the site rose from 13 tonnes in 2022 to 17 tonnes in 2024, according to EA records.
Benzene, which is used to make some plastics, is carcinogenic to humans and causes leukaemia. According to the World Health Organization there is no safe level of exposure.
In an inspection report from March, the EA recorded several permit breaches in relation to the benzene emissions. The document states benzene is a carcinogen and it is “reasonably foreseeable that the deficiencies in the management system will cause multiple emissions, that when agglomerated, may result in a significant impact on the environment or human health until resolved through compliance”.
Failure to comply with an environmental permit is a criminal offence.
A Huntsman spokesperson said the benzene emissions were not illegal and were “fully compliant with our permit conditions”.
However, the EA told the Guardian: “We are considering further enforcement action with our legal team in relation to these permit breaches and have informed the UK Health Security Agency and the Health and Safety Executive so that they can assess any public or occupational health risks”.

articles.title: Thunderstorms and flash flood risk on final day of UK heatwave
articles.raw_rss: More places in southern and eastern England are expected to reach heatwave criteria on Tuesday but cooler temperatures are on the horizon.
articles.raw_meta: More places in southern and eastern England are expected to reach heatwave criteria on Tuesday but cooler temperatures are on the horizon.
articles.jina_text:
Pershore in Worcestershire and Cavendish in Suffolk hit three consecutive days of heatwave threshold temperatures on Monday and it is expected more parts of southern and eastern England will reach heatwave criteria on Tuesday.
Amber and yellow heat health alerts, external are in effect across much of England until 09:00 BST Wednesday, with temperatures expected to reach more than 30C in some areas. 
The intense heat will be short lived though as a change in the weather pattern is on the way from midweek.



When will the heatwave end?





Image caption, 

The highest temperatures will be felt in southern and eastern England on Tuesday




During Tuesday, a cold front will move southwards across the Midlands and into south-east England. However, it is unlikely to deliver any meaningful rainfall.
Some areas in the far south-east, including London, Essex, Kent and Surrey, are unlikely to receive any rain at all.
This is a pattern that has become all too familiar in recent weeks, as the UK experienced its driest and sunniest July on record.
Areas of low pressure have tracked to the north of the UK, bringing below-average rainfall and consistently failing to deliver any meaningful rain further south.



Flash flooding and hail risk












To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be played
Figure caption, 

Scattered thunderstorms will develop through the day on Tuesday




Low pressure which has recently brought rainfall to Scotland, Northern Ireland and parts of northern England will bring scattered showers and thunderstorms on Tuesday and into Wednesday. However, this is unlikely to alleviate the current drought.
A yellow thunderstorm warning has been issued by the Met Office for parts of Northern Ireland on Tuesday.
It runs until 21:00, when up to 30mm of rain in an hour or two is possible, along with strong winds and the chance of hail.
Areas that do see a heavy downpour are at risk of flash flooding.
The scorched ground, dry grass and soil caused by the lack of rain is likely to cause significant pooling and runoff, as rainfall struggles to get absorbed during brief bursts of heavy rain.
Hail may accompany the most intense downpours which could come as a surprise following the predominantly hot and dry conditions.
Hail is most common in summer months as it needs to develop inside towering cumulonimbus clouds, which are often spawned by intense heat at ground level.






Why thunderstorms follow hot weather





28 May



Will there be another heatwave?




Image source, Joe Sene/PA Wire




Following one of the driest and hottest stretches of weather in the UK's history, the indications are that August is likely to bring more of the same.
Forecast models suggest low rainfall and above average temperatures will continue for much of the UK, meaning it is unlikely that any of the hosepipe bans affecting more than 20 million people in England and Wales will be lifted soon.

Nine animal rights campaigners are pursuing legal action against the Metropolitan Police, alleging they were wrongfully arrested during the King's Coronation in May 2023.
The women, ranging in age from 20 to 64, claim officers mistakenly identified them as members of Just Stop Oil while they attended a non-violent workshop organised by Animal Rising.


The group, which includes students, medical professionals and teachers, is being represented at the High Court by Hodge Jones & Allen. Their lawyers maintain there was "no intelligence linking the women or Animal Rising to Just Stop Oil".
The Met Police denies any wrongdoing and is contesting the claim. The women were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.

Nine animal rights campaigners are pursuing legal action against the Metropolitan Police, alleging they were wrongfully arrested during the King's Coronation in May 2023 | 
PA


The Animal Rising workshop took place roughly five miles from the Coronation ceremony itself. According to the group, between 15 and 20 officers, described as predominantly male, entered the premises and accused them of being affiliated with Just Stop Oil, which had been using the same building.
The women claim they were subjected to full body searches before being detained for periods of up to 14 hours after their arrest. Each of them remained under investigation for several months, only receiving their phones back at the end of August 2023, when they were informed there was insufficient evidence to pursue further action.
A CrowdJustice fundraising page has been set up to support the legal challenge, which centres on the Met's claim that intelligence linked the group to Just Stop Oil.

articles.title: Heatwave forces Romania to blast Danube river to help nuclear plant
articles.raw_rss: Water levels in the River Danube, which flows through ten countries from Germany to the Black Sea, have dropped to just 23 centimetres in Budapest as severe drought grips central Europe.
articles.raw_content:
Water levels in the River Danube, which flows through ten countries from Germany to the Black Sea, have dropped to just 23 centimetres in Budapest as severe drought grips central Europe.
Hungary is preparing to completely shut down its only nuclear power plant later this week as the river becomes too shallow to supply water for cooling.
The record low levels have also triggered a state of emergency in Romania, where energy conservation measures have led to two car-makers halting production.
Meanwhile, extreme weather is gripping much of the world including wildfires in the US and floods in India, while England and Wales is just coming out of the driest July on record. These heat extremes are made more likely because of carbon pollution from burning fossil fuels.

articles.jina_text:
Romanian naval forces carried out a controlled explosion to help redirect vital cooling water from the drought-hit Danube to the country’s last working nuclear ⁠reactor, while neighbouring Hungary ​said it may be able to eke out two more days of power from its only atomic plant.
Hungary and Romania have been forced to shut down nuclear reactors cooled by the Danube for the first time, as record-low water levels deepen fears of an energy crisis across the region.

Romania has declared a nationwide state of emergency throughout August stemming from a decline in electricity production after record low Danube river levels led to the shutdown at the Cernavodǎ nuclear plant.
The Danube operation used 180kg of explosives, the Adevărul newspaper reported, to move a large rock restricting the flow of water in a blast that sent a tower of water ⁠into the air. The extraordinary measure underlined the scale of the crisis in Europe, where heat and drought have lowered river levels and raised concerns about water supplies, river transport and power generation.
“Any day past Wednesday or Thursday that the nuclear power plant functions is a gain,” Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruțǎ, said on Monday. “A day of it functioning is three times more efficient than the costs of this operation.”

Experts said the controlled explosion would allow authorities to build a temporary dam, diverting more water into the channel serving Cernavodǎ’s remaining reactor.


With both countries’ sole nuclear plants at reduced ⁠capacity, Hungary and Romania are increasingly relying on expensive power imports as heatwave conditions increase demand for electricity. Both countries use water ​from the Danube as coolant for their reactors.
At Paks, Hungary’s Soviet-era nuclear power station, output has been reduced. The 44-year-old plant, which normally generates almost half of the country’s electricity, is operating at less than half its capacity. Authorities ‌earlier said they might have to ‌shut Paks as early as Sunday, but later said it could operate at its reduced capacity until Monday ‌or Tuesday, offering a small reprieve for the power supply.
Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, said the plant was expected to be fully shut down next week. With the Danube forecast to remain too shallow for the reactors’ cooling systems, the closure could last for several weeks.
“An energy crisis situation could arise beginning Monday,” he posted on X. “Coordinated steps and restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences. We are counting on everyone!”
He added: “Today and maybe tomorrow the last turbine producing 240 megawatts can keep working. This is very good news, as the complete shutdown of the plant can be avoided on one of the days with the ‌highest consumption.”

Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England, the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has warned as a heatwave was forecast to continue into next week.
The UK’s Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued heat health alerts for eight regions of England, with temperatures set to rise above 30C in parts of the country. UKHSA said rising temperatures may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult, and now in many areas they do not have access to water as irrigation is being restricted due to drought.

It is the third drought in five years and farming groups say this is the new normal for agriculture in Britain. Wheat farmers say their crop is half its normal height, and England is seeing its earliest ever harvest as farmers battle to salvage what they can of their produce.
In some areas it has not rained for over a month, while multiple record-breaking heatwaves have hit the country since early summer, drying out the soil.
Tom Bradshaw, the NFU president, said this could lead to food shortages and he had asked the prime minister to take action. He told BBC Radio 4 that farmers should be given tax breaks to build water storage systems on their land to prepare for the years ahead.
“Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well,” he said. “It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products.”
Climate breakdown is exacerbating extreme weather conditions such as droughts. This summer the Met Office has reported that England had just 8% of its average rainfall for July and it is likely to be confirmed as the driest July on record.


About 23 million people across England and Wales are under a hosepipe ban. The dry weather has fuelled devastating wildfires across the country, most recently in Suffolk.
UKHSA has issued amber heat health alerts for the East Midlands, the east of England, the south-east and London regions from 9am on Monday to 9am on Wednesday. The north-west, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and the south-west regions will be under a yellow alert during the same period.
Bradshaw said: “Let’s draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK.”
Cereals such as wheat and barley have been particularly affected, the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) said.
Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006, with many farmers across the south and east of England completing harvest two to three weeks ahead of the long-term average.

Graham Readfearn






One expert described Nationals leader Matt Canavan’s claim of land used for clean energy as ‘plain wrong and plain silly’ 
 
 
 
Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates 





It was all incredibly matey as Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan strode into cattle saleyards near Rockhampton to meet Karl Stefanovic for a “great net zero debate”.
Perhaps a month was long enough for the pair to have forgotten Stefanovic’s left arm being draped around British far-right figure Tommy Robinson and the fawning interview he had given to the anti-Islam activist (an interview that ultimately saw him part company with longtime employer, Nine).

But there they were, the Coalition’s two leaders, on another episode of the former morning television darling’s eponymous podcast and YouTube show.
“Good on you, Karl,” said Canavan, in front of the assembled crowd. “Wonderful to be here with you,” said Taylor.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email
Then the “debate” began. Strictly speaking, a debate is where you have opposing views that can thrash out an issue in front of an audience to inform public discourse.


But this was not that.
Instead it was an entirely one-sided platform for the Coalition to demonstrate their contempt for large renewable energy projects and to repeat tropes about “net zero” and electricity costs.
Two Tasmanias?
The Nationals leader told the audience that 12m hectares of land would be needed for “solar, wind and transmission lines”.
“That’s two Tasmanias’ worth of this stuff across our nation,” Canavan said.
Canavan said this figure had come from the “very smart people” at Net Zero Australia – a research partnership of the University of Melbourne, the University of Queensland, and Princeton University.
So what did NZAu actually find?
In its most recent reporting, NZAu said 2m ha – not 12m – would be needed for renewable energy and transmission infrastructure (slide 36 in this pdf if you want to follow along at home) to help Australia reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions.

This “direct footprint” would be about 500,000ha – 24 times less than Canavan’s “two Tasmanias’”.

August usually sends me into an anxious funk, but I think I’ve worked out how to handle 2026’s terrifying heat and apocalyptic images





Unfortunately for hairdressers, “How’s your summer going?” is a loaded question this year. Even basking lizards and barbecue obsessives are wavering in their sun worship as cataclysmic wildfires engulf our nearest neighbours (and threaten the UK), Wales and parts of England experience drought, and farmers issue dire warnings about our food supply in the near future. Rescue centres are filling up with dehydrated hedgehogs and the Environment Agency is having to rescue fish. Lazy, joyful, sunscreen-scented days are giving way to stifling, existentially terrifying ones spent skulking in the dark (assuming you don’t need to be out in the extreme heat, as many workers do), sweatily scrolling through apocalyptic images.
Vanity Fair has decreed it’s a “sad-girl summer”, highlighting the female singer-songwriters soundtracking the myriad anxieties of an “undeniably cruel” 2026 season, but it’s not just the girlies who are sad – many of us are struggling and we still have August to survive. How?

I’m a veteran of sad-girl summers (possibly Sad summers – some people get seasonal affective disorder when it’s hot and bright). For years, July and August have sent me into an anxious, distressed funk, afflicted by brain shutdowns that leave me useless for days at a time. That means I’m ahead of the curve in finding little survival tactics, so here are some, if you find yourself struggling with what used to be the carefree, fun season.
Treat yourself like a beloved dog
Look at canine heatwave advice and apply it to yourself. Little walks in the coolest parts of the day, frozen treats, wet towels and top-ups of chilled water will all help maintain your mental equilibrium. Naps won’t hurt either.
Start your day with a book
Defer your engagement with the horrors – they’ll still be there in half an hour; they don’t need to be the first thing to hit your eyeballs. Immerse yourself in something – anything – engaging offline for a while. If your concentration is shot and you fear you will struggle not to scroll, the novelist Naomi Alderman is running a brilliant reading version of Couch to 5K on her Substack.
Take up a temporary hobby
Distract yourself with something ultra-low stakes. Last year, I tried growing melons. My misshapen babies were inedibly disgusting, but tending them helped during my twitchiest hours. This summer’s project is “making elaborate salads that would cost £17 in London”. Every day, I craft a photogenic heap of fancy, fibremaxxing fodder, take a picture, save it on my phone in a folder called “lunch” (that I will delete in September), then feast. It’s daft, but it is the high point of many distressing, scratchy-brained days.

Relentless UK heatwaves turn ‘green and pleasant land’ brown


Visible impact of warming climate is impossible to ignore across landscapes that have been starved of rainfall




Half of England and the whole of Wales are officially in drought and July is set to be the driest month on record as extreme heat intensified by the climate crisis continues to grip the UK and Europe this summer.
The announcements this week by England’s Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales mark the third such event over the past five years, and come in the wake of four record-breaking heatwaves since May which have fuelled huge wildfires and left farmers, wildlife and protected habitats running out of water.



View image in fullscreen
A two-arched stone bridge thought to date to 1800 at the Llwyn-onn reservoir in the Taf Fawr valley in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales was exposed by low water levels last week. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
England had just 7% of the long-term average rainfall for July and southern England just 1%, damaging greenery in parks, protected land and sports fields. The dry spell has also led to shrinking rivers and lakes: the Thames at Reading has recorded its lowest ever level.


Water companies are not currently expecting a threat to drinking water supplies, as record winter rainfall means reservoirs are still close to expected levels, but approximately 23 million people across England and Wales are under a hosepipe ban.
The visible impact is impossible to ignore: vast swathes of William Blake’s “green and pleasant land” are now brown and dry. The Met Office predicts that the climate crisis will make UK summers 1C-6C (1.8F-10.8F) hotter and up to 60% drier by 2070, compared with 1990.


View image in fullscreen
The Cerne Abbas giant in Dorset. Left image taken in August 2023, right taken August 2026. Composite: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images


Both adaptation to and mitigation of the effects of a warming planet are urgently needed, said Dr Chloe Brimicombe, a climate scientist at the University of Oxford.
“This summer has been a compounding of dry weather,” said Brimicombe, “leading to droughts and hot weather and high temperatures leading to heatwaves with these conditions also leading to wildfires. It is a strong indication that we need better long-term planning. Climate change is not a future problem; it’s a challenge for right now.”
As the climate crisis supercharges “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather, the UK and Europe are seeing back-to-back heatwaves that encourage vegetation to grow but then dry it out, producing ideal fuel for fires.

Council leaders say crumbling infrastructure and lack of water are jeopardising government’s plans for new homes




The government’s housebuilding agenda is hitting the stark reality of a lack of water and crumbling infrastructure across the east and south-east of England.
Half the country was declared to be in serious drought this week, for the second consecutive year, with the Environment Agency warning of dire consequences for the economy, environment and wildlife.

Environmental pressures are already extreme in the south and east of England. In one area where increased housing numbers are being demanded, fenlands are close to collapse from over-extraction of water; in another, chalkstreams are having to be artificially maintained.



Some water companies are clear there is “insufficient” water for new homes, a situation exacerbated by crumbling infrastructure.
“We cannot magic up more water,” said Paul Harvey, the Independent leader of Basingstoke and Deane council, which is being told to build more than 1,000 houses a year in Hampshire. “They say ‘build, baby, build’ but it is something we cannot just wave a wand and do.

French wildfires that have scorched an area more than four times the size of Paris and forced thousands of tourists to flee could end the traditional European holiday – with Britons flocking to “coolcations” instead.



More than 250,000 people have been evacuated from affected regions, including 4,000 residents and visitors from tourist sites west of Bordeaux on Tuesday.



The wildfires around Bordeaux, in the south-west of France, have been described by President Emmanuel Macron as the country’s most severe fire-related crisis since the Second World War.

Southern Europe ‘no longer a relaxing summer escape’ 
Dr Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said: “These wildfires are a stark reminder that France, as well as Spain, Italy and other European holiday destinations, are becoming increasingly exposed to extreme heat and risk. 
“It is likely that as our climate continues to warm, 50℃ will be experienced for the first time somewhere in Europe in the years to come.” 
A survey by InsureandGo, conducted in May, found that three in four UK holidaymakers believe that traditional hot spots such as France, Spain, Greece and Cyprus will be too hot to visit by 2030. 
“Southern European holidays will no longer be a relaxing summer holiday escape,” said Ilan Kelman, professor of disasters and health at University College London.



 

France has been hit by drought conditions following a heatwave and water shortages (Photo: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters) 
Earlier this week, tourists were urged by a French official from Bordeaux’s surrounding region of Gironde not to visit until the “situation is under control”. 
Peter Sammonds, professor of geophysics and climate risks at UCL, said: “The human body struggles to cope in 33℃ weather, and for some it can be even lower.  
“Going forward, British tourists need to become aware of these risks, similar to how they would when travelling somewhere like Egypt or Cyprus. Tourists do not think about these things when going to France.” 
In 2024, France was the second-most visited country by British tourists, amassing 9.3 million visits, according to the Office for National Statistics. 
The wildfires have been influenced by El Niño, a Pacific weather pattern that increases global temperatures.  
But Bentley said: “El Niño will add extra warmth to the global climate, but it isn’t the main reason Europe is experiencing these extremes.” 
“The overwhelming driver is long-term climate change, which is increasing the likelihood and intensity of the conditions we’re seeing across southern Europe.”

Hundreds of fish in a city centre river are believed to have died as a result of the recent heatwave and contamination from drainage water.
Residents and wild swimmers were horrified to find them washed up on Saturday, appearing to gasp for air, in the River Wensum through Norwich.
Local river campaigner Sarah Eglington said the scenes were "absolutely heartbreaking".
The Environment Agency said it believed the incident was the result of the recent heatwave - ultimately depleting the river's oxygen - and because heavy rainfall on Thursday had likely flushed in contamination from surface water drainage systems.
A spokesperson explained that high temperatures created the conditions that "significantly" reduced dissolved oxygen levels in the water.

‘Climate change kills’: Pedro Sánchez speaks plain truth to Spain’s deniers


PM has long history of speaking out on realities of global heating but political opponents remain unnmoved




Just over four years ago, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, visited a small town in the south-western region of Extremadura that had been affected by one of the wildfires devouring tens of thousands of hectares of land across the country.
That summer’s blazes had left two people dead in the northern region of Castilla y León and another man there fatally burned after the excavator he was using to try to dig a firebreak to protect his town was swallowed up by the flames. A street-sweeper in Madrid had collapsed and died from heatstroke while on shift in soaring temperatures that summer. The paramedics who tried to save him noted that his body temperature was 41.6C (107F).

“I want to make something very clear,” the prime minister told reporters in Extremadura that day in 2022. “Climate change kills: it kills people, as we’ve seen; it also kills our ecosystem, our biodiversity, and it also destroys the things we as a society hold dear – our houses, our businesses, our livestock.”


View image in fullscreen
Pedro Sánchez (centre) visits fire-affected areas of Extremadura in 2022. Photograph: Ballesteros/EPA
Earlier this week – amid wildfires that have consumed more than 180,000 hectares (428,915 acres) of land in the first seven months of 2026 – he repeated the same blunt warning.


“The climate emergency kills,” he said on Monday. “And that’s why it’s not enough to address the consequences, which we do; what we have to do is reduce its causes, anticipate its effects, and, consequently, better prepare our country to protect people’s lives.”
Just as he has been one of the most vociferous European leaders when it comes to criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza and Donald Trump’s war in Iran - and defending the benefits of immigration – so Sánchez has long deployed unvarnished language to raise awareness of the climate emergency.
On the face of it, that may come as little surprise: as a country on the southern frontier of the world’s fastest-heating continent, Spain is becoming increasingly vulnerable to the effects of the climate emergency, be they droughts, desertification, erratic weather patterns, heavy rains or wildfires.

In Oregon and Washington, low humidity and powerful winds have put officials on alert for wildfire spread




A heatwave scorching the western US region has elevated the risk of hazardous fire conditions particularly in parts of Oregon and Washington, where low humidity and powerful winds have put officials on alert for wildfire spread.
The National Weather Service has forecast blistering temperatures through early next week that could climb from 110F to 120F across the south-west. In the Pacific north-west, highs reaching into the 90s are expected in the days to come.

Several western states are dealing with devastating wildfire seasons.
In Oregon, about 1.8m acres (730,000 hectares) have reportedly been torched, as of July.
A rare “particularly dangerous situation” was assigned to a red flag warning in effect for eastern Oregon on Saturday, where weather officials have forecast gusts of wind from 30-40mph.

In Washington, more than 1,000 fires have torn through roughly 425,000 acres, a level of destruction not seen since 2021, according to the state department of natural resources. State officials are also working to contain 12 large fires that cumulatively have set more than 200,000 acres ablaze.
The active wildfire year comes as the state is in a drought, owing to insufficient snowpack. The state depends on snowmelt to fill its rivers and reservoirs, but this year, precipitation fell more as rain than as snow, according to the Washington department of ecology.
The confluence of drought conditions, dangerous heat and strong winds led Washington governor Bob Ferguson to temporarily ban outdoor burning through the end of September.
“Our firefighters are already stretched thin across the state, and with more heat and wind expected this weekend and for the rest of the summer, any new spark on our tinder dry landscapes can lead to another devastating wildfire,” said Dave Upthegrove, the state’s commissioner of public lands, in a news release.

Research makes clear that global warming is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe. Yet the climate crisis has largely disappeared from the political agenda, with many Democrats who once described it as an existential threat now shying away from talking about it.

Now US activists are pushing back against this trend of “climate hushing”, arguing it is misguided. During the summer’s federal recess, during which lawmakers leave the nation’s capital to work directly within their home states or districts, demonstrators organized by the environmental advocacy coalition Climate Action Campaign are calling on representatives to put climate back on the political agenda.
“The long history of the climate movement proves that we move fastest when there’s real pressure from the grassroots,” said Bill McKibben, the environmental author and activist who co-founded climate non-profit 350.org, “All the evidence shows those grassroots are as worried about [the] climate crisis as they ever were.”

articles.jina_text:
In these days of extreme weather events, it seems odd to say that the US needs a big landslide. But a landslide defeat for President Donald Trump in November’s midterm elections is exactly what is required if the country is to start reversing his deliberate and rapid erosion of its democracy.
The respected Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Institute at Gothenburg University argues that in 2025 the US saw one of the most rapid declines in liberal democracy on record. “Democracy in the USA,” says its Democracy Report 2026, “is now at its worst in 60 years.” As the imperial republic marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, the danger seen at the very beginning of its constitutional order by anti-federalists such as Patrick Henry – that of an overmighty president abusing his executive power in an attempt to become a new king – has come closer than ever before.



V-Dem analysts note that in 2025 Trump issued no fewer than 225 executive orders whereas the Republican-controlled Congress passed just 49 laws, most of them on minor issues such as “To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to modify the rules for postponing certain deadlines by reason of disasters”. The Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025, crafted to advance the so-called unitary executive theory, is, according to the project’s own tracker, more than halfway to completion – helped by rulings from the supreme court.
An important chapter in any would-be autocrat’s playbook is fixing the next election. It seems Trump is hard at work on this one too. Beside outrageous levels of partisan gerrymandering (responded to in kind by the Democrats in some places) there are multiple attempts to deny the vote to groups more likely to vote Democrat, whether by restricting mail-in ballots, demanding on-the-spot documentary proof of US citizenship or other legal and procedural devices. If the 3 November election result were to be close in a number of congressional districts that might swing control of the House of Representatives, Trump and the Republicans would pull out every stop to disqualify or exclude Democrat victors.
Hence the imperative of a landslide. As Hungary showed this spring, if the popular revulsion towards an incumbent is sufficiently widespread, and channelled into turning out to vote, it sweeps away all the obstacles that the would-be autocrat puts in place – and those obstacles were, taking all in all, larger in the Hungarian case than they are here. The election may not be fair; it may not even be entirely free; but the result is still irrefutably plain for all to see.


Now, if you ask who is doing most to bring about an anti-Trump landslide, the answer is clear: Donald Trump. After he campaigned on bread-and-butter issues for ordinary Americans, the combination of his tariffs and his war of choice in the Middle East has actually increased the cost of living – most visibly, in petrol prices for motorists. An El Niño climate pattern typically brings dangerous heat domes and hurricanes to the Pacific but experts have added to the list of threats this year: sea snakes and sharks.
White sharks - known commonly as great whites - are swimming off the California coast in greater numbers this year thanks to hotter ocean temperatures linked to this year’s supercharged El Niño.
"We expect to see all kinds of weird tropical things come up with this warm water," Douglas McCauley, director of the Benioff Ocean Initiative at the University of California, Santa Barbara, told USA Today.





One of those weird things is the venomous and tropical yellow-bellied sea snake.
A bite from this sea snake can lead to paralysis and death in just hours without treatment, according to the Australian Museum.

El Niño - the warm phase of a global climate pattern - has been tied to shifting populations of sea lions, turtles and fish in the past, too. There were Hammerhead shark bites reported off the Southern California coast during the 2015-2016 El Niño event, according to KNBC.
"We saw this fin and then it dove," kayaker Kyle Hudgins told the station after his friend Dylan Marks was bitten while kayaking near Santa Monica.

Andy Burnham’s new Energy Secretary has previously backed calls for frequent flyers to be charged a green tax on plane tickets. 
Miatta Fahnbulleh was chief executive of the New Economics Foundation (NEF) think-tank between 2017 and 2023, which advocated for a levy to help limit carbon emissions from flights. 
A report published in 2021 backed charges potentially worth hundreds of pounds to target people who fly regularly, replacing the current Air Passenger Duty (APD) system.

 
In the same year, the now Energy Secretary told The Independent that the Conservative government – which had announced a cut to APD on domestic flights – should be “raising, not cutting, taxes with a frequent flyer levy”. 
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has insisted that a frequent flyer levy is “not government policy,” and there is no suggestion Fahnbulleh will push for it as a minister – or that the Government is considering introducing one. 
But Fahnbulleh’s past support offers insight into her views on the environment and into the case made by campaigners and the Government’s own advisers for cutting emissions from frequent flying. 
What is a frequent flyer levy? 
Currently, the Government charges Air Passenger Duty (APD) on every passenger aged over 16 who departs from a UK airport. The aircraft operator pays the fee, but the cost is usually passed on to passengers through their ticket price.



 
The exact charge depends on the cabin class, type of aircraft and destination, and ranges from £8 for a domestic economy flight to £1,141 for a long-haul trip on a private jet. 
In 2021, the NEF and Possible climate charity proposed scrapping APD and replacing it with a new frequent flyer levy. 
Under the proposal, a passenger’s first leisure flight of the year would be tax-free, with each subsequent flight charged progressively more. Business flights would be taxed from the first trip. 
The idea, in short, is that a small number of wealthier, frequent flyers are responsible for a disproportionate share of flying-related emissions, so should pay more. In contrast, people who fly only once a year should pay less than they do now. 
The Government’s own climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), also proposed a similar system in 2019. 
However, their preferred model works differently. Rather than a flat rate that rises purely with the number of flights taken, it would charge per tonne of carbon emitted, meaning the cost also depends on the distance flown and the class of ticket bought. 
As with NEF’s proposal, the first flight of the year would be exempt under this model too.

articles.title: Heat pumps can make your home ‘easier to sell’ – but won’t always add value
articles.raw_rss: A heat pump may not add its full installation cost to your property’s price, but experts say it could make an energy-efficient home more attractive to buyers
articles.raw_meta: A heat pump may not add its full installation cost to your property’s price, but experts say it could make an energy-efficient home more attractive to buyers
articles.jina_text:
As homeowners look for ways to cut their energy use and reduce their reliance on gas, increasingly, heat pumps are becoming an attractive alternative to gas boilers. They produce fewer carbon emissions and, in the right property, can help to lower heating costs. Government support has made the upfront investment more manageable, too, with eligible households able to claim up to £7,500 towards installation, through the Boiler Upgrade Scheme.
But a heat pump is still a major home improvement, and the financial calculation goes beyond running costs alone. Homeowners may also wonder whether installing one will make their property more appealing to future buyers, improve its energy performance certificate (EPC) rating or even increase its eventual sale price.
The answer is not straightforward. A well-designed system in an efficiently insulated home could become a valuable selling point, but experts caution that buyers rarely pay a pound-for-pound premium for energy upgrades. Here, surveyors, property specialists and housing experts explain what homeowners should consider before investing.

How heat pumps work
Heat pumps work by extracting heat from the air or ground outside and using it to provide heating and hot water within a property. Unlike conventional boilers, which cycle on and off as temperatures rise and fall, heat pumps operate more steadily, maintaining a consistent indoor temperature. 





Although electricity costs more than gas per unit, a heat pump can typically generate around three units of heat for every unit of electricity it consumes. This means energy bills can be lower, particularly when combined with off-peak electricity tariffs or solar panels.
Heat pumps can cost between £8,000 and £15,000 to install but upfront installation costs have become more manageable, thanks to the government's Boiler Upgrade Scheme, which offers homeowners up to £7,500 in grants. The average price to replace a gas boiler is around £2,000 to £3,000. With incentives in place, many homeowners are now asking whether a heat pump is also a genuine investment when it’s time to sell their property.

A shift in greener thinking
Paul Broadhead, head of mortgage and housing policy at the Building Societies Association, believes attitudes towards greener homes have changed significantly.


"What the volatility in energy prices has really focused people on is how much a property is going to cost to run. If you go back 15 or 20 years, the only focus for buyers was how much the property was going to cost to buy."

articles.jina_text:
A man inspects damage to his property in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Spain. Photograph: Damian Torres/AP
View image in fullscreen
A man inspects damage to his property in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Spain. Photograph: Damian Torres/AP


ECB official warns climate crisis poses growing threat to ‘core financial stability’


Exclusive: As wildfires rage, Frank Elderson says more work needed to assess risk from collapse of ecosystem services




A senior policymaker at the European Central Bank has said the climate emergency and the breakdown of nature poses a dramatically growing risk to the global economy.
Frank Elderson, a member of the ECB’s executive board, said the eurozone lender of last resort was stepping up its monitoring of the financial risks linked to the destruction of “ecosystem services”, which are nature-related processes or assets that support human activity.

“These services are not stable but they are in rapid decline. That’s why we talk about the climate and nature crises,” he said. “So knowing that dependency, and knowing those exposures by the banks, we come to the conclusion that this is relevant.”
Across France and Spain, wildfires have raged amid record-breaking temperatures, torching land, businesses and homes, in an emergency that will carry a heavy economic cost beside the direct human toll.



In an interview with the Guardian before the current devastation across Europe, Elderson said it was clear the rising frequency of natural disasters linked to global heating pos a threat to financial stability.
He said more work needed to be done to assess the risk from the collapse of ecosystem services, as reliance on nature was more complicated to map than the impact of a single extreme weather event.
Ecosystem services are defined as any benefit that can be drawn from a natural structure or process – for example, water can be used as a raw material, an energy source through hydropower, or for transportation. It is also a habitat for marine life critical for food production, and a basis for recreational services.
“Nature-related risks can pose material economic and financial risks, including through their impacts on credit risk, growth, inflation and – over the long-term – potential financial instability,” Elderson said.
“I did interviews [previously] saying, you know, if you destroy nature, you destroy the core on which our economies depend. And that got people’s attention. This is not some kind of a flower-power, tree-hugging exercise. This is core economics. This is core financial stability, core price stability.”


As the supervisor responsible for Europe’s largest banks, the ECB has launched a programme of work to assess how the escalating damage to ecosystem services could expose the financial system to risk.
The central bank plans to publish analysis later this year investigating how “ecosystem degradation pathways” could translate into credit loss dynamics for the eurozone’s banks.

articles.raw_meta: António Guterres says strengthening El Niño will help push the world’s climate crisis into ‘uncharted territory’
articles.jina_text:
India’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of the world as a stronger El Niño weather system is taking hold, weather experts have warned.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the strengthening El Niño was “adding fuel to a planet already on fire” and pushing the world into “uncharted territory”.

The El Niño system will strengthen from August to October, which will bring higher temperatures globally, with increasing rainfall in some regions while others suffer drought, according to data and forecasts released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Friday.
Marine heatwaves have already shocked scientists this year and are set to intensify: the WMO said temperatures were likely to exceed 2.9C above normal in several regions.



“The Pacific waters driving it have never been this warm this early in an El Niño, and temperatures are still increasing,” Guterres said. “[This year] risks shattering every seasonal record, and driving even more severe effects worldwide. We are in uncharted territory.”
The risk of a weakened monsoon, which brings the rain on which Indian farmers rely, was highlighted as the forecast gave an “enhancement in the probability for below-normal rainfall”, which would produce increased drought, floods and wildfire risk around the Indian Ocean basin. Drier conditions are also likely across parts of equatorial Africa to the west of the Horn of Africa, across the south and east of Australia, large parts of South America and in North America.
Higher than normal rainfall is expected in southern Europe, central Asia and the Horn of Africa and south-eastern South America.
Extreme weather has already caused havoc around the world this summer, with record-breaking heatwaves beginning in May in the UK, and wildfires across France and Spain that have destroyed villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.


View image in fullscreen
A destroyed house after wildfires in the village of Le Porge, Gironde, France. Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/The Guardian


Scientists have warned this year of the development of an El Niño, a weather system in the Pacific that frequently affects temperatures and rainfall around the world. Some El Niño years in the past have been relatively mild, but scientists have said that this year’s has been supercharged by the climate crisis.
Warmer waters – earlier in the year than usual and with water temperatures still increasing – have led to predictions of a “super El Niño” forming. The WMO does not use this term, but has said that the weather system developing is likely to be significantly stronger and more intense than usual. Friday’s forecasts were the organisation’s latest update, covering August to October.
